title: The Little Gas Station That Welcomed Everyone
summary: Route 66, the famous highway that once ran more than 2,000 miles from Chicago to Los Angeles, is celebrating its 100th anniversary. Along the way, one small gas station in Oklahoma tells a big story about kindness in hard times. During the Jim Crow era, Black families traveling Route 66 faced a serious problem: most restaurants, gas stations, and motels would not serve them. Families had to carry their own food and gas, and they used a travel guide called the Green Book to find safe places to stop. But there was one place they could always count on. The Threatt Filling Station in Luther, Oklahoma, just east of Oklahoma City, offered fuel, food, and a place to sleep. According to the National Trust for Historic Preservation, it was the only known Black-owned and operated gas station along the whole highway. Allen Threatt Sr. built the original station in 1915, after moving from Alabama to Oklahoma as part of the Great Migration. When Route 66 was founded in 1926, the trickle of cars past his land became a steady stream. After the first wooden building burned down, Threatt replaced it with a sandstone building made to look like a small, welcoming house. 'Grandpa took care of whatever they needed to have,' said Linda Fisher, Threatt's granddaughter. 'If they didn't have any food, they fed them. If they needed some kind of shelter or blankets, Grandpa and Grandma made sure they got those kinds of things.' The station became a community hub, with dances, barbecues, and even baseball games by players from the Negro Leagues. But when the new interstate highways were built, traffic on Route 66 faded, and the station closed in the 1970s. For decades it sat empty. Then Threatt's grandchildren decided to save it. With grants and hard work, they have restored the building's outside, and visitors can now stop by, learn the family story, and see the ceramic gas pumps from the 1940s. The family hopes to add an RV park, a restaurant, and a new baseball diamond. 'We're all standing on Grandpa's shoulders,' said Edward Threatt, another grandchild leading the restoration. 'We're just trying to do them proud.'
why_it_matters: The station shows how one family's kindness helped travelers in unfair times, and saving it keeps that story alive for the next generation.
